feedback: If a learner expects the orbiting ball to need an outward or balancing force, point out the only force shown is gravity pointing inward; the net force is not zero — it constantly changes the direction of motion.
If they think a faster ball should fly straight off immediately, show that gravity still curves its path — only beyond escape speed does it leave for good.
If they say the orbiting ball is 'weightless' or 'free of gravity', highlight that gravity is fully acting the whole time; that is exactly what bends the path.
activities.intendedInsight: An orbit is continuous free fall: in this idealised model (no air resistance), the only force is gravity pulling inward, curving otherwise-straight sideways motion into a closed loop. Too slow and the ball arcs down and hits the ground; from the circular-orbit speed up to just below escape speed it orbits (a circle at first, then longer ellipses as speed rises); at or above escape speed it leaves for good. Orbit is continuous with everyday falling, not a separate phenomenon.
learnerActions: Set a launch speed for a cannonball fired horizontally from the top of a tall mountain and predict where it will land before firing.
Fire at a gentle speed and watch it arc out and hit the ground a short distance away.
Nudge the speed higher repeatedly, observing the ball land further each time and the curve of its fall starting to echo the curve of the planet.
Find the critical speed at which the ball falls all the way around without reaching the ground and loops back — a stable orbit.
Push faster still to stretch the circle into an ellipse, then faster again until the ball escapes entirely.
In your own words, state what the ball is actually doing when it orbits (it is only falling — it is just going sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth).
activities.title: Newton's cannonball: tune launch speed until it orbits

feedback: If a learner says the Moon astronaut has less mass, correct that mass is the same everywhere — only weight changes because g is smaller on the Moon.
If they confuse which quantity is in newtons, note weight is a force (N) found by multiplying mass (kg) by g (N/kg).

Check the arithmetic: a 40 kg mass weighs about 400 N on Earth (40 × 10); on the Moon, where g is about 1.6 N/kg, it weighs only about 64 N (40 × 1.6); on a hypothetical world with g half of Earth's it would weigh about 200 N. The half-g world is an illustrative example, not the Moon.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass (amount of matter) is invariant; weight = mass × g changes because gravitational field strength g differs between planets. The same astronaut weighs less on the Moon though their mass is unchanged.
learnerActions: Stand a fixed mass on a scale and read its weight on Earth.
Switch the planet selector to the Moon, then Jupiter, each time reading the new weight while noting the mass number never changes.

Using weight = mass × g (with g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth), calculate the weight of a 40 kg mass on Earth; then work out its weight on the Moon using the Moon's g ≈ 1.6 N/kg, and compare with a hypothetical world of half Earth's g.
State explicitly what changed (weight, because g changed) and what stayed the same (mass, the amount of matter).
activities.title: Same mass, different weight: weight = mass × g across worlds

feedback: If a learner says 'only planets or big things have gravity', explain gravity acts between all masses; it is simply too weak to notice between small objects.
If they think gravity needs air, note gravity acts in the vacuum of space — it does not depend on an atmosphere.
If they think only one body is pulled, show the force diagram acting equally on both bodies.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity is universal: the same attractive force operates between an apple and Earth, Earth and Moon, Sun and planets; it is stronger for larger masses and weaker at greater distances. It is not special to Earth's surface, does not require an atmosphere, and acts equally on both bodies in a pair.
learnerActions: Examine a two-mass attraction diagram showing the force acting on BOTH bodies (apple–Earth, Earth–Moon, Sun–planet).
State the common rule: every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is stronger for bigger masses and weaker the farther apart they are.
Explain why we do not notice the pull between two everyday objects (it is real but far too weak to feel), and why planets' pull is obvious (huge mass).
Decide whether gravity could act in a vacuum with no air, and justify the answer.
activities.title: Universality: the same force everywhere

feedback: A learner saying 'there is no gravity up there' holds the dominant misconception; reteach that gravity at the ISS is ~90% of surface strength and floating is free fall together.
A learner saying 'gravity and speed cancel to zero force' misreads free fall; the net force is the unbalanced inward gravity constantly changing direction of motion.
A learner saying their mass changes on the Moon has the mass–weight conflation; mass is fixed, weight = mass × g changes with g.

A full response explains orbit as continuous free fall with gravity as the centripetal force, affirms gravity is universal, distinguishes fixed mass from g-dependent weight, and transfers to a different planet or orbit.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation: apply weight = mass × g numerically and articulate orbit as continuous free fall with gravity providing the centripetal force. Both 'no gravity' and 'gravity provides the orbit' predict floating, so the reasoning must be stated to distinguish them.
learnerActions: Complete weight = mass × g calculations for a fixed mass on different planets (give the missing weight for Earth, Moon and Jupiter).
Answer the diagnostic: 'Astronauts on the Space Station float as if weightless. Does that mean there is no gravity up there? Explain what is really keeping the station in orbit.'

Give the two-part answer: there IS gravity (roughly 90% of surface strength at the Station), and floating is because the station and astronauts are in continuous free fall, with gravity supplying the inward (centripetal) force that curves their motion into an orbit.
Answer the probe: 'If gravity in orbit were really zero, what path would the Station follow — a circle or a straight line?' and justify (a straight line, because no force means no curving).
activities.title: Check and consolidate: weight calculations and the orbit diagnostic
